items.summary:
XS::libbrotli versions before 1.2.1.0 for Perl bundle a brotli library with an out-of-bounds write in the decoder.

Affected versions compile a bundled brotli into static archives that dependent XS modules link against at build time, rather than using the system library. The bundled copy, 1.0.7 or 1.1.0 across the range, carries the decoder out-of-bounds write described in CVE-2026-111497. Version 1.2.1.0 updates it to brotli 1.2.1.

XS::libbrotli has no Perl interface, so the decoder is reached through any dependent module that decompresses untrusted data with it. An attacker supplying a crafted brotli stream can corrupt decoder state, disclose memory, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. Upgrading the system brotli does not remediate this.

items.summary:
A logic error in Epiphany's site permission handling can cause camera and microphone access to be granted when the user only approves a different permission.

In src/ephy-window.c, set_permission() stores the user's Allow/Deny choice after a WebKit permission dialog. Types CLIPBOARD and WEBSITE_DATA_ACCESS are not stored by ephy_permission_is_stored_by_permissions_manager(), so control fell into an else-if that was written as:

  } else if (EPHY_PERMISSION_TYPE_ACCESS_WEBCAM_AND_MICROPHONE) {

Because that expression is a non-zero enum constant, the branch always ran for those types and wrote EPHY_PERMISSION_PERMIT for both ACCESS_WEBCAM and ACCESS_MICROPHONE for the site origin. The user only saw a Clipboard or Website Data Access dialog.

A malicious site that obtains approval for clipboard or third-party storage access can afterwards use getUserMedia without a further camera/microphone prompt, exposing audiovisual confidentiality.

Requirements: the victim must visit a malicious page and click Allow on a clipboard or website-data-access prompt.

Affected: Epiphany >= 45.0 (bug present at least through 51.x).
Fixed: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/epiphany/-/merge_requests/2249 (commit 480c3648).
Upstream: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/epiphany/-/work_items/2976
Reporter acknowledgment: Fernando Munoz

items.summary:
A file overwrite vulnerability exists in Epiphany when installing WebExtension packages from .xpi files.

In src/webextension/ephy-web-extension-manager.c, decompress_xpi_thread() used libarchive with archive_read_support_format_all() (and filters), so the installer did not require a real ZIP. A TAR file named *.xpi was extracted. TAR supports hard-link entry types; with Epiphany's archive_write_disk options (including ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM), a crafted hard-link target can cause an attacker-chosen existing user-writable file to be truncated and overwritten with attacker-controlled content and mode bits, without a dedicated warning dialog, when the user installs or opens the crafted .xpi.

This is related to but separate from the ZIP-slip path traversal fixed as CVE-2026-77679 (#2922 / MR !2143).

Requirements: the victim must install or open a malicious WebExtension (.xpi).

Affected: Epiphany >= 47.0 (WebExtension XPI install path).
Fixed: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/epiphany/-/merge_requests/2248 (commit 0cc9ab55 — only enable ZIP format support).
Upstream: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/epiphany/-/work_items/2988

Exploitation requires the site to have double opt-in enabled with "Disable login for unactivated customers" explicitly set to No (a non-default configuration), public customer registration enabled, and the original activation token redeemed within its one-day expiry window.

## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server decompresses uploaded pipeline archives without adequately bounding expanded data in affected versions. A small ZIP or gzip-compressed tar archive can consume disproportionately large amounts of memory while the server locates or reads the pipeline file, potentially exhausting API-server resources and interrupting service.

Multipart pipeline and pipeline-version upload processing decompresses the archive before namespace authorization, so a caller who can reach those endpoints does not need a successful pipeline-create authorization decision to trigger the issue. External authentication and network controls can restrict reachability. URL-import handlers authorize before fetching and decompressing a remote archive.

The amount of expansion needed to exhaust memory depends on deployment resource limits and concurrent activity; no particular archive is guaranteed to crash every deployment.

## Remediation

Upgrade the API server to **[Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/releases/tag/2.18.0)**. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

[PR #14171](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/14171) bounds compressed input and extracted pipeline data. [PR #14186](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/14186) strengthens the total tar traversal budget, including metadata and skipped entries. The 2.18 release also includes configurable upload and specification limits; operators should review the shipped settings and resource budget. These controls address pipeline archive amplification and do not establish general HTTP-body, temporary-disk, concurrency, or CPU limits.

Until upgrading, restrict access to upload and import endpoints and apply deployment-level request and resource controls. A compressed upload-size limit alone does not prevent decompression amplification. Regression tests cover compressed input, selected-entry boundaries, and tar traversal budgets; no deployed-server OOM test was performed for this assessment.

## Credit

[bugbunny.ai](https://bugbunny.ai) discovered and reported the issue. Ayush Gupta ([@Ayush-kathil](https://github.com/Ayush-kathil)) authored the archive fixes in #14171 and #14186, with Jeff Spahr ([@jeffspahr](https://github.com/jeffspahr)) contributing regression coverage to #14171.

[@BrianWillows](https://github.com/BrianWillows) later submitted a mixed report that included source analysis of pipeline-archive decompression.
items.title: Kubeflow Pipelines: Pipeline archive upload allows decompression bomb to exhaust server memory

## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server's `GET /apis/v1alpha1/runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id}/log` handler retrieves logs without authorizing the caller against the selected run. A caller who can reach the backend and knows a victim run ID and a suitable pod or node identifier can read live or archived logs using the API server's permissions.

For live logs, the vulnerable handler also accepts the supplied node ID as a pod name in the run's namespace without verifying that the pod belongs to the run. Depending on the API server's pod-log permissions, a known run ID can therefore permit reading the `main` container logs of an unrelated pod in that namespace. Logs may contain sensitive workload data or credentials.

The affected handler does not authenticate the request itself. An external authentication gate or network policy can restrict reachability; public ingress exposure and unauthenticated enumeration of run IDs are not assumed.

## Remediation

Upgrade the API server to **[Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/releases/tag/2.18.0)**. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

[PR #13684](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/13684) authorizes the caller with the `readLog` verb before retrieving live or archived logs. For live logs, it also verifies that the pod's `pipeline/runid` label matches the requested run. Custom Kubernetes roles must grant `readLog` on `runs` in the `pipelines.kubeflow.org` API group; the bundled viewer and editor roles include it. Shared read access alone does not grant log access.

Until upgrading, restrict access to the backend log endpoint. Focused regression tests cover authorization denial, HTTP identity propagation, pod/run mismatch, archive retrieval, and cancellation; no new deployed-cluster end-to-end test was performed for this assessment.

## Credit

[bugbunny.ai](https://bugbunny.ai) discovered and reported the issue. Nayyar ([@naruto-lgtm](https://github.com/naruto-lgtm)) authored the fix in #13684.

[@patchmyday](https://github.com/patchmyday), [@thesecguy45](https://github.com/thesecguy45), [@VitoCrl](https://github.com/VitoCrl), [@Grg0rry](https://github.com/Grg0rry), [@arpitjain099](https://github.com/arpitjain099), and [@BrianWillows](https://github.com/BrianWillows) made later submissions concerning the run-log authorization gap. **MUTEDCYBERSECURITY S.L.** separately reported a synthetic two-tenant reproduction, including the unrelated-pod log path.

### Summary

`Joi.string().email({ multiple: true })` takes quadratic time to split a value that contains a long run of whitespace. One request with 100 KB of spaces blocks the Node.js event loop for several seconds, which causes a denial of service.

### Details

When the `multiple` option is set, the `email` rule splits the value into addresses with a regular expression that removes whitespace on each side of the separator:

```js
const regex = new RegExp(`\\s*[${options.separator ? escapeRegex(options.separator) : ','}]\\s*`);
// ...
const emails = options.multiple ? value.split(regex) : [value];
```

`String.prototype.split` tries a match at each position of the value. At each position inside a whitespace run, the leading `\s*` reads the rest of the run, does not find a separator, and backtracks through all of it. A run of `n` whitespace characters without a separator therefore costs `n²` steps. This applies to the default separator and to all custom `separator` values.

The fix lets the leading whitespace match start only at the beginning of a whitespace run, so the split is linear:

```js
const regex = new RegExp(`(?:(?<!\\s)\\s+)?[${options.separator ? escapeRegex(options.separator) : ','}]\\s*`);
```

The split results do not change. The regular expression is now built only when `multiple` is set.

Every `joi` release from `17.1.1` up to and including `17.13.8`, and from `18.0.0` up to and including `18.3.0`, is affected. Every `@hapi/joi` release from `16.0.0` is affected.

Workarounds for users who cannot upgrade:

- Add `.max()` before `.email()`, for example `Joi.string().max(1000).email({ multiple: true })`. The `max` rule then rejects long values before the `email` rule runs.
- Do not use the `abortEarly: false` option with this schema. With `abortEarly: false`, the `email` rule runs even when the `max` rule fails.
- Do not use `.trim()` as a workaround. It removes only the whitespace at the start and at the end of the value.

### Proof of concept

```js
const Joi = require('joi');

const schema = Joi.string().email({ multiple: true });
for (const n of [25000, 50000, 100000, 200000]) {
    const start = Date.now();
    schema.validate(' '.repeat(n));
    console.log(`${n} spaces: ${Date.now() - start} ms`);
}
```

Output on `joi@18.3.0` (Node.js 26):

```text
25000 spaces: 244 ms
50000 spaces: 887 ms
100000 spaces: 3349 ms
200000 spaces: 13579 ms
```

Output on the patched version:

```text
25000 spaces: 0 ms
50000 spaces: 0 ms
100000 spaces: 0 ms
200000 spaces: 1 ms
```

Over HTTP, send the whitespace in a field that the route validates with this schema:

```http
POST /invite HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"emails": "<100000 spaces>"}
```

### Impact

This is a denial of service by CPU exhaustion. It affects each application that validates untrusted input with `Joi.string().email({ multiple: true })` and that has no length limit before the `email` rule. One request with 100 KB of whitespace blocks the Node.js event loop for several seconds, and the server cannot process other requests during that time. The attacker needs no authentication when the route is public, and a small number of concurrent requests can keep the service unavailable.

minimatch 10.2.6 contains an attacker-controlled pattern amplification in firstPhasePreProcess() when optimizationLevel >= 2.

researcher: Reid Downing (b1nv0id)
files: 

- src/index.ts: 690-770
- src/index.ts: 780-796

issue:
input-controlled growth of globParts during first-phase preprocessing, followed by quadratic second-phase processing.

the **/../ transformation clones a globparts entry and appends the clone to the same globparts array:
```
parts.splice(gs, 1)
const other = parts.slice(0)
other[gs] = '**'
globParts.push(other)
```
this occurs inside a do...while (didSomething) fixpoint loop, allowing generated entries to be processed again.

the expanded globparts array is subsequently processed by secondPhasePreProcess(), which performs pairwise comparisons:
```
for (let i = 0; i < globParts.length - 1; i++) {
  for (let j = i + 1; j < globParts.length; j++) {
    this.partsMatch(...)
  }
}
```
an attacker who can supply a glob pattern can therefore cause additional pattern entries to be generated during preprocessing, followed by quadratic pairwise processing, resulting in excessive cpu and memory consumption.

### Summary

In glob 13.0.6, an aborted async walk rejects or emits an error but continues recursively reading directories in the background.

The root cause is that abort branches in src/walker.ts call cb() without returning. As a result, callers that rely on signal or AbortSignal.timeout() to bound glob traversal cost can still incur filesystem I/O and CPU work after the request has already been rejected.

### Details

This was reproduced on glob v13.0.6 (commit e80cb38ae60d6cbff9e75f39032a994858994d35).

The README documents that the signal option cancels the glob walk. However, in src/walker.ts, the following methods call cb() when this.signal?.aborted is true but do not return:

- GlobUtil.walkCB()
- GlobUtil.walkCB2()
- GlobUtil.walkCBSync()
- GlobUtil.walkCB2Sync()

Example vulnerable pattern:

if (this.signal?.aborted) cb()

Because execution continues after cb(), the walker still reaches processor.processPatterns(), readdirCB(), and recursive walkCB2() calls.

The issue was directly demonstrated against v13.0.6. A source-history review shows the same missing-return pattern is present in tagged releases from v9.0.0 through v13.0.6.

The issue affects both glob() and globStream().

Recommended fix:
Change each abort branch to return immediately:

if (this.signal?.aborted) return cb()

### Proof of concept

Environment:
- Linux x86_64
- Node.js v22.23.3
- npm 10.9.9
- glob 13.0.6

Reproduction steps:

1. Install the affected package:
   npm init -y
   npm install glob@13.0.6

2. Run the attached PoC:
   node poc/abort-continues-work.mjs

The PoC aborts after the first readdir() call, waits briefly, and counts how many more directory reads happen after the promise has already rejected.

Observed output on the vulnerable version:

{
  "rejection": "Error: probe-abort",
  "readdirCalls": 1365,
  "readdirCallsAtReject": 5,
  "readdirCallsAfterReject": 1360
}

Expected behavior:
readdirCallsAfterReject should be 0.

A second PoC using AbortSignal.timeout() also reproduces the issue:

{
  "rejection": "TimeoutError: The operation was aborted due to timeout",
  "readdirCalls": 133,
  "readdirCallsAtReject": 1,
  "readdirCallsAfterReject": 132
}

The same test against a patched build with return cb() in the four abort branches stops immediately:

{
  "readdirCalls": 1,
  "readdirCallsAtReject": 1,
  "readdirCallsAfterReject": 0
}

### Impact

This is an availability issue.

Applications that expose globbing over attacker-influenced patterns or attacker-controlled directory trees and use AbortSignal / AbortSignal.timeout() as a traversal budget can still perform significant filesystem I/O and CPU work after a request has already timed out or been canceled.

Repeated timed-out requests can stack background glob walks and degrade worker throughput or service availability.

No confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.
items.title: Glob: AbortSignal cancellation bypass allows post-timeout filesystem traversal

## Description

### Summary

RFC 7592 (OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Management Protocol) lets a previously registered client read, update, or delete its own registration, authenticated by a `registration_access_token` issued specifically to that client at registration time. The entire security model of this protocol depends on the server verifying that the token presented in the request actually belongs to the client identified in the request, not merely that the token is valid for some client.

Authlib's `ClientConfigurationEndpoint` implements the control flow correctly in structure, calling `authenticate_token`, then `authenticate_client`, then `check_permission`, and treats all three as abstract methods that "Developers MUST implement in subclass." The problem is that the documented example implementations for these methods, taken together exactly as written, never perform the one check that matters: binding the authenticated token to the specific client being accessed. A developer who implements these methods by following the provided examples ends up with a complete authorization bypass on this endpoint.

### Details

`authenticate_client`'s documented example (`authlib/oauth2/rfc7592/endpoint.py`):

```python
def authenticate_client(self, request):
    """Read a client from the request payload.
    Developers MUST implement this method in subclass::

        def authenticate_client(self, request):
            client_id = request.payload.data.get("client_id")
            return Client.get(client_id=client_id)

    :return: client instance
    """
    raise NotImplementedError()
```

This looks the target client up purely by the `client_id` supplied in the request payload, with no reference to the token at all.

`check_permission`'s documented example, in the same file:

```python
def check_permission(self, client, request):
    """Checks whether the current client is allowed to be accessed, edited
    or deleted. Developers MUST implement it in subclass, e.g.::

        def check_permission(self, client, request):
            return client.editable

    :return: boolean
    """
    raise NotImplementedError()
```

This checks a property of the target client alone (whether it is generally "editable"), again with no reference to `request.credential`, the authenticated token object returned earlier by `authenticate_token` and stored on the request specifically so that later steps can check it:

```python
def create_configuration_response(self, request):
    token = self.authenticate_token(request)
    if not token:
        raise AccessDeniedError()

    request.credential = token

    client = self.authenticate_client(request)
    ...
    if not self.check_permission(client, request):
        raise UnauthorizedClientError(...)
```

`request.credential` is set specifically so that a binding check can be performed downstream, but neither documented example ever reads it. Following both examples as written produces an implementation where the only requirements to access, modify, or delete a client's registration are: possessing any valid registration_access_token for any client, and knowing or guessing the target `client_id`.

This is meaningfully different from how the equivalent example is written for the token introspection endpoint (RFC 7662) elsewhere in the same codebase, which does correctly demonstrate checking the authenticated caller's own identity (`authlib/oauth2/rfc7662/introspection.py`):

```python
def check_permission(self, token, client, request):
    """Check if the request has permission to introspect the token. Developers
    MUST implement this method::

        def check_permission(self, token, client, request):
            # only allow a special client to introspect the token
            return client.client_id == "introspection_client"
    """
```

In that endpoint, `client` represents the already-authenticated caller (verified through normal client credential authentication earlier in the flow

## Summary

In pyasn1 through 0.6.4, decoding a constructed BIT STRING with many fragments repeatedly shifts and copies the entire value accumulated so far. For fixed-size fragments, CPU time grows quadratically with the encoded input size. An application that passes sufficiently large, attacker-controlled ASN.1 data to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion during `decode()`; no conversion or formatting of the decoded value is required.

The BER and CER decoders reach this path for constructed BIT STRING values, with or without an `asn1Spec`. The DER decoder rejects constructed BIT STRING in schema-less decoding, but its schema-driven path accepts a **definite-length** constructed BIT STRING when given a matching `asn1Spec` and reaches the same vulnerable code. Constructed BIT STRING is not valid DER; this DER exposure is due to decoder permissiveness. DER rejects the indefinite-length form.

This is a separate decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER accumulation fixed in [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj).

## Technical details

In the 0.6.4 [`BitStringPayloadDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L173-L301), both the [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L237-L255) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L275-L301) fragment loops call `BitString.fromOctetString(..., prepend=bitString)` for every fragment. [`fromOctetString`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/type/univ.py#L614-L627) shifts the growing `SizedInteger` left by the fragment's bit length and ORs in the fragment. Shifting an ever-larger Python integer for each fixed-size fragment makes total work O(n²) for n fragments. The fragments are siblings, so the decoder's nesting-depth limit does not constrain their count; its limit on the number of length octets does not prevent the demonstrated inputs.

In 0.6.4, DER's [tag-driven map](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L40) disables constructed BIT STRING, while its schema-driven type map retains the inherited decoder that permits it. This explains why a schema-less DER rejection is not a negative result for all DER decoding.

Under [X.690](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en), a conforming CER constructed BIT STRING uses an indefinite-length outer encoding and primitive fragments with 1000 contents octets except possibly the last. That form reaches the affected indefinite-length loop. DER requires primitive string encoding, although the schema-driven pyasn1 decoder accepts the definite-length constructed example below.

## Impact

An application is exposed when untrusted input can reach one of the affected decoder paths and its input limits admit enough fragments. The work occupies the decoding thread or worker and may cause denial of service. Whether the input is network-accessible or unauthenticated depends on the calling application. This advisory makes no claim that every application using pyasn1, or any particular protocol implementation, accepts such input.

## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)

The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER values trigger the issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted values could occupy a finite decoder-worker pool and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not claim that every application is network-exposed or fully unavailable; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).

## Summary

In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a binary-encoded ASN.1 REAL with a large mantissa can consume CPU time quadratic in the mantissa length. The BER, CER, and DER decoders all use the affected `RealPayloadDecoder`. An application is exposed when it passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 containing a REAL value to one of these decoders, either without an `asn1Spec` or with a schema that includes REAL. The work occurs inside `decode()`; the application does not need to convert, print, or otherwise use the resulting REAL object.

This is distinct from [CVE-2026-59886](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hm4w-wwcw-mr6r), which concerns converting an already-decoded REAL to a Python float. That issue was fixed in 0.6.4 and its advisory states that decoding alone does not trigger it.

## Root cause and affected components

For binary REAL values, [`RealPayloadDecoder.valueDecoder` in v0.6.4](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L535-L603) builds the mantissa one octet at a time:

```python
p = 0
while chunk:
    p <<= 8
    p |= chunk[0]
    chunk = chunk[1:]
```

Each shift processes an integer that grows with the mantissa; with byte strings, each slice also copies the remaining suffix. Repeating both operations for every octet makes decoding quadratic in mantissa size. The decoder's [eight-octet length-field limit](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1704-L1717) does not impose a practical mantissa-size limit for the inputs demonstrated below. [CER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/cer/decoder.py#L51-L62) and [DER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L23-L31) reuse the BER REAL payload decoder, so all three paths reach this loop.

The vulnerable loop is present in every available repository release tag inspected, from v0.2.1 through v0.6.4. Runtime measurements below were made on v0.6.4; older releases were checked for the loop, not benchmarked individually.

A comparatively small REAL value can hold a decoder worker on one CPU core for seconds or longer. The attacker must be able to supply data that the application sends to an affected decoder, and application-level input limits may reduce exposure. The demonstrated effect is CPU exhaustion during decoding; this advisory does not assert a network endpoint, unauthenticated access, or an affected downstream application by itself.

## Summary

In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a constructed OCTET STRING or character string made of many fragments can spend disproportionate CPU time repeatedly copying the accumulated value. A separate indefinite-length `ANY` path has the same problem while collecting the encoded components. The work grows roughly quadratically with the number of fixed-size fragments, although the input and decoded value grow linearly. An application that lets an attacker supply such ASN.1 input to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion.

The affected string paths are available in BER and CER. The DER decoder also accepts certain *non-DER* constructed strings: a definite-length constructed OCTET STRING when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.OctetString`, and constructed character strings such as UTF8String even without a schema. Indefinite-length `ANY` is affected in BER and CER when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.Any`; DER rejects indefinite lengths.

This is a distinct decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER/RELATIVE-OID accumulation addressed by [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj). It has the same complexity class, but the OID fix in 0.6.4 did not change these string or `ANY` loops.

## Technical details

In the [v0.6.4 BER decoder](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py), `OctetStringPayloadDecoder` appends each decoded fragment to a growing `bytes` value with `header += component` in both its [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L338-L351) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L368-L387) constructed forms. [`AnyPayloadDecoder.indefLenValueDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1403-L1430) similarly uses `chunk += component`. In the exercised paths, each concatenation copies an increasingly large prefix. For `N` fixed-size fragments, the total copied data grows with `1 + 2 + ... + N`, or O(N²).

The OCTET STRING decoder is also the base class of the decoders for UTF8String, NumericString, PrintableString, TeletexString, VideotexString, IA5String, GraphicString, VisibleString, GeneralString, UniversalString, BMPString, ObjectDescriptor, GeneralizedTime, and UTCTime. These types inherit the same constructed-string reassembly path.

The [DER decoder's OCTET STRING restriction](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L49) replaces the tag-driven decoder, but its schema-driven `TYPE_MAP` retains the BER-derived decoder. Thus `der.decode(data)` rejects a constructed OCTET STRING, while `der.decode(data, asn1Spec=univ.OctetString())` accepts its definite-length form and reaches the accumulation loop. DER does not replace the inherited character-string decoders, so a constructed UTF8String is also accepted without `asn1Spec`. These inputs violate [X.690's DER string-encoding rule](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en) and should not be described as valid DER encodings.

### Summary

When an application decodes attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER data without an ASN.1 schema, a container with many distinct long tag IDs can cause quadratic CPU use. Repeated inputs can exhaust CPU and reduce service availability.

### Details

ConstructedPayloadDecoderBase._decodeComponentsSchemaless inserts every decoded component’s TagSet into a growing set, although it only needs to distinguish one tag set from two or more. Attacker-chosen tag IDs can have colliding TagSet hashes, making each later insertion compare against an increasing number of earlier tags. This path is present in v0.6.4 and is inherited by the CER and DER decoders. The proposed fix stops growing the classification set after it contains two distinct tag sets, while retaining every decoded component and its order.  On v0.6.4 with CPython 3.12.10, increasing the collision input from 3,200 to 6,400 components raised decode CPU time from 0.438 to 1.747 seconds; a comparable control rose from 0.031 to 0.065 seconds. Both inputs decoded successfully with the expected values and an empty remainder.

### Proof of concept

Run this outside the repository checkout in a fresh Python 3.12 environment with pyasn1==0.6.4 installed:

```python
import sys
import time

from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder
from pyasn1.type import univ


def enc_tag(tag_id):
    groups = [tag_id & 0x7f]
    tag_id >>= 7
    while tag_id:
        groups.append((tag_id & 0x7f) | 0x80)
        tag_id >>= 7
    return b'\xbf' + bytes(reversed(groups))


def payload(tag_ids):
    body = b''.join(enc_tag(tag_id) + b'\x03\x04\x01A'
                    for tag_id in tag_ids)
    length = len(body).to_bytes((len(body).bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big')
    return b'\x30' + bytes([0x80 | len(length)]) + length + body


for count in (3200, 6400):
    cases = (
        ("collision", [32 + i * sys.hash_info.modulus
                       for i in range(count)]),
        ("control", [(1 << 70) + i for i in range(count)]),
    )
    for name, tag_ids in cases:
        wire = payload(tag_ids)
        start = time.process_time()
        value, remainder = decoder.decode(wire)
        cpu_seconds = time.process_time() - start

        assert type(value) is univ.Sequence
        assert len(value) == count and remainder == b''
        for position, tag_id in enumerate(tag_ids):
            component = value.getComponentByPosition(position)
            assert component.asOctets() == b'A'
            assert component.tagSet[-1].tagId == tag_id

        print(count, name, len(wire), round(cpu_seconds, 3))
```

### Impact

Applications that pass attacker-controlled bytes to schemaless BER, CER, or DER decoding can spend disproportionate CPU time on a relatively small, valid input. The demonstrated impact is availability; no confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.

### Summary

`asn1.oidToDer()` did not range-check the first two arcs of an OID string, so an OID such as `0.42.840.113549.1.1.1` or `4294977127.18.840.113549.1.1.1` was encoded as the DER of a different OID (here rsaEncryption, `1.2.840.113549.1.1.1`). This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-66030. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

X.690 section 8.19 encodes the first two arcs of an OID as one subidentifier, `40 * arc1 + arc2`, where the first arc is 0, 1 or 2 and the second arc is at most 39 when the first is 0 or 1. `asn1.oidToDer()` in `lib/asn1.js` computed that value with no range check and wrote it with `putByte()`, which keeps only the low 16 bits. Out-of-range first arcs therefore produced the encoding of a different OID: `0.42.840.113549.1.1.1` gives `40 * 0 + 42 = 42` and `4294977127.18.840.113549.1.1.1` wraps to 42, both the first byte of rsaEncryption. The fix for CVE-2025-66030 (GHSA-65ch-62r8-g69g, node-forge 1.3.2) added a 32-bit check for the later arcs only.

A related encoding bug made valid OIDs with a first subidentifier above 127 (`2.48` and higher, e.g. `2.999`) encode and decode incorrectly, because the first subidentifier was always written and read as a single byte.

The fix rejects out-of-range first arcs and encodes and decodes the first subidentifier in base 128 like the others (the latter from public PR #1148).

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. `asn1.oidToDer()` throws for OIDs with out-of-range first arcs, and the first subidentifier is encoded and decoded correctly.

### Workarounds
Validate OID strings from untrusted input before passing them to node-forge: the first arc must be 0, 1 or 2, and the second arc at most 39 when the first arc is 0 or 1.

### Credits
Reported by wzc. The first subidentifier encoding fix is from PR #1148 by @spokodev.

### Proof of concept

    var forge = require('node-forge');
    var der = forge.asn1.oidToDer('0.42.840.113549.1.1.1');
    console.log(der.toHex()); // 2a864886f70d010101
    console.log(forge.asn1.derToOid(der)); // 1.2.840.113549.1.1.1

On 1.4.0 the out-of-range OID string encodes to exactly the DER of rsaEncryption (the same happens with `4294977127.18.840.113549.1.1.1`). On 1.4.1 `oidToDer()` throws "Invalid OID; the first two arcs are out of range.".

Regression tests are in tests/unit/asn1.js ("should reject OIDs with out of range first arcs").

### Impact

Applications that accept OID strings from untrusted input, check or authorize them as strings, and then encode them with node-forge (for example when building certificates, CSRs or other ASN.1 structures from user-supplied extension or attribute OIDs) can be made to emit a different, trusted OID than the one that was checked. Parsing DER is not affected. There is no confidentiality or availability impact.

### Summary
The `forge.http` client stored cookies from `Set-Cookie` response headers in a plain object keyed by cookie name and path. A malicious server could use the cookie name `__proto__` to add properties to `Object.prototype`, use inherited names such as `constructor` to add properties to `Object`, and send an empty cookie value to delete `Object.prototype` properties. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`client.setCookie()` in `lib/http.js` stored a cookie with `client.cookies[cookie.name][cookie.path] = cookie`, creating `client.cookies[cookie.name]` only when `!(cookie.name in client.cookies)`. Both values come from the server's `Set-Cookie` header via `response.getCookies()`. Because `in` also sees inherited properties:

- a cookie named `__proto__` skipped the initialization, `client.cookies['__proto__']` returned `Object.prototype`, and the cookie path was written as a new `Object.prototype` property, visible on every object;
- a cookie named `constructor` wrote onto the global `Object` function the same way;
- a cookie with an empty value calls `client.removeCookie(name, path)`, which used the same `in` checks and then `delete client.cookies[name][path]`, so `Set-Cookie: __proto__=; path=toString` deleted `Object.prototype.toString`. This path skipped the cookie's secure-flag and domain checks, so it also worked for `http://` clients.

`forge.http` is not loaded by `require('node-forge')`. It is included in the `forge.all` browser bundle and is used with a socket pool, for example by `forge.xhr`.

The fix uses own-property checks for the cookie store and ignores cookies named `__proto__` or with the path `__proto__`.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Cookies from a server can no longer add or remove properties of `Object.prototype` or `Object`.

#### Workarounds
Don't use `forge.http` or `forge.xhr` with servers that aren't trusted, or filter `Set-Cookie` headers named `__proto__`, `constructor` or other `Object.prototype` property names before they reach the client.

#### Credits
Reported by @arunmozhivarman-dtx and @Dremig.

### Proof of concept
A server response for a `forge.http` client (`http.createClient({url: 'https://...', socketPool: ...})`) containing:

    Set-Cookie: __proto__=evil; path=polluted

On 1.4.0, after the client processes the response, `({}).polluted` is the cookie object. With `Set-Cookie: __proto__=; path=toLocaleString`, `Object.prototype.toLocaleString` is deleted (for `http://` and `https://` clients). On 1.4.1 these cookies are ignored and `Object.prototype` is unchanged.

Regression tests are in tests/security/ghsa-6wvx-3r32-xmcg.js.

### Impact
Applications that use the `forge.http` client (directly, or through `forge.xhr` in the `forge.all` browser bundle) against a server that can be malicious are affected. The server can add properties to `Object.prototype` and `Object` for the whole JavaScript realm, which can change application logic that reads properties from plain objects, and can delete built-in `Object.prototype` methods, breaking the page or process. Applications that don't use `forge.http` are not affected.

### Summary
The forge TLS client's check for a missing server certificate read the wrong property and never ran. A malicious TLS server, or an on-path attacker who removes the server's Certificate message, can make `connection.process()` throw a `TypeError`, which crashes applications that use the forge TLS client. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
After ServerHelloDone, `tls.handleServerHelloDone()` in `lib/tls.js` is meant to reject a server that sent no certificate with a fatal `insufficient_security` alert, after consulting the application's `verify` callback. The check tested `c.serverCertificate`, which is never set (the certificate is stored as `c.session.serverCertificate`), so it never ran. The client state machine allows ServerHelloDone directly after ServerHello, so the handshake continued to `tls.createClientKeyExchange()`, which reads `c.session.serverCertificate.publicKey` and throws a `TypeError` on the null certificate. The exception propagates out of `connection.process()` without calling the `verify` or `error` callbacks.

There is no authentication bypass: without a server certificate the client cannot build its RSA key exchange, so the handshake cannot complete.

The fix reads `c.session.serverCertificate` and always fails the handshake in that case, still calling `verify` so the application can customize the alert. Failing even when `verify` returns `true` is needed because the key exchange requires the certificate.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. The TLS client fails the handshake with an `insufficient_security` alert when the server sends no certificate.

#### Workarounds
Catch exceptions thrown by `connection.process()` in the code that feeds it network data, and close the connection when one occurs.

#### Credits
Reported by @arpitjain099.

### Proof of concept
Connect a forge TLS client (`forge.tls.createConnection({server: false, ...})`) to a server whose first flight contains ServerHello and ServerHelloDone but no Certificate message. For example, run a forge TLS server and remove the Certificate handshake message (type 11) from its first flight before passing it to the client's `process()`.

On 1.4.0 the client's `process()` throws "TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'publicKey')", and the `verify` and `error` callbacks are not called. On 1.4.1 the client calls `verify` with `insufficient_security` and no certificates, calls `error` with "No server certificate provided. Not enough security.", sends a fatal alert and closes the connection.

Regression tests are in tests/unit/tls.js ("missing server certificate").

### Impact
Applications that use the forge TLS client (`forge.tls.createConnection` with `server: false`) are affected. A malicious server the application connects to, or an on-path attacker who can modify the unauthenticated handshake, can make the client throw from `connection.process()`. Since `process()` is normally called from a socket data handler, the uncaught exception terminates a Node.js process. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact. Applications using Node.js's own TLS implementation are not affected.

### Summary
`pem.decode()`, which every node-forge API that parses PEM input uses, split messages with a regular expression that takes polynomial time on input without a matching END line, and parsed encapsulated headers with regular expressions that take quadratic time on long header lines. A remote attacker can block the Node.js event loop for seconds to minutes with a crafted input of a few tens of kilobytes. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`pem.decode()` in `lib/pem.js` found PEM messages with this regular expression:

    /\s*-----BEGIN ([A-Z0-9- ]+)-----\r?\n?([\x21-\x7e\s]+?(?:\r?\n\r?\n))?([:A-Za-z0-9+\/=\s]+?)-----END \1-----/g

The optional headers group and the body group are adjacent, lazy, and share characters (whitespace and the base64 alphabet), and the match must end with an END line whose label equals the BEGIN label (`\1`). When no such END line follows, the engine tries every split of the text between the two groups, for every label split and at every BEGIN line in the input. The work grows polynomially with the input length (roughly cubic for repeated BEGIN/END lines with mismatched labels, quadratic for a BEGIN line followed by many newlines).

The encapsulated header parsing in the same function had two smaller quadratic cases: trimming each header line with `/\s+$/`, and an unanchored header regex `([\x21-\x7e]+):...` that retries at every position of a long line without a colon. These are reachable when a message does match.

All PEM entry points call `pem.decode()`, including `pki.certificateFromPem()`, `pki.privateKeyFromPem()`, `pki.publicKeyFromPem()`, `pki.certificationRequestFromPem()`, `pki.encryptedPrivateKeyFromPem()`, `pki.decryptRsaPrivateKey()` and `pkcs7.messageFromPem()`.

The fix replaces the message regular expression with a scanner that indexes the END lines once and matches each BEGIN line in linear time, finding the same messages as before. The one difference: a label containing `-----` (`-----BEGIN A-----B-----`) was matched as `A-----B` if possible; now only the shortest label, `A`, is used. RFC 7468 labels can't contain `--`. Header parsing now trims lines with a loop and only starts a header match at the beginning of a run of printable characters, which gives the same result.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. PEM messages and encapsulated headers are now parsed in linear time.

#### Workarounds
Rejecting untrusted PEM input larger than a few kilobytes before passing it to node-forge limits the delay but doesn't remove it: on 1.4.0, about 7 KB of crafted input blocked for 0.4 s, and 29 KB for 24 s.

#### Credits
Reported by Ahmed Mokhtari (@AhmedMokhtari), @mwlik and @imenyoo2, and independently by @offset, @bibu123456 (coordinated by @Kayiz-PT), and @Mucahic.

### Summary

`BigInteger.prototype.modInverse()` in node-forge's bundled jsbn library enters an infinite loop when the value or the modulus is negative, for example when a negative public exponent is passed to `forge.pki.rsa.generateKeyPair()`. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-33891 (GHSA-5m6q-g25r-mvwx), which handled only a zero value. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`bnModInverse()` (`lib/jsbn.js`, exposed as `forge.jsbn.BigInteger.prototype.modInverse`) implements the binary extended Euclidean algorithm (Handbook of Applied Cryptography, Algorithm 14.61), which is defined for positive integers. With a negative operand the loop cannot terminate: `rShiftTo` is an arithmetic shift, so a negative value never moves towards zero, and the loop's exit condition (`u` reaching zero) is never met. The calling thread spins at 100% CPU indefinitely; in Node.js this blocks the event loop. Memory does not grow.

node-forge 1.4.0 fixed CVE-2026-33891 (GHSA-5m6q-g25r-mvwx) by returning zero early when `this.signum() == 0`, although its changelog describes the check as "<= 0". Negative values were not covered, and a negative modulus was never handled. Every negative input that did terminate already returned zero.

Within node-forge, RSA key generation is the only path to a negative operand: the caller's public exponent `e` becomes `BigInteger.fromInt(e)`, and `state.e.modInverse(state.phi)` is called with it. `gcd()` works on absolute values, so the coprimality checks pass and the loop is reached. Any exponent other than 3 or 65537 uses the pure JavaScript implementation, even when `forge.options.usePureJavaScript` is not set. RFC 8017, Section 3.1 requires the RSA public exponent to be at least 3.

Values that node-forge parses (DER, PEM, JWK, PKCS#12, X.509, TLS) are always read as unsigned integers and cannot produce a negative operand.

The fix makes `modInverse()` return zero when the value or the modulus is zero or negative, as it already does when no inverse exists. Results for positive inputs are unchanged.

This issue was reported by wzc.

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. `modInverse()` now returns zero when the value or the modulus is zero or negative.

### Workarounds
- Pass only fixed, valid RSA public exponents (e.g. 65537) to key generation, or validate caller-supplied exponents first: an odd integer `>= 3`.
- Do not call `BigInteger#modInverse()` with negative operands. Reduce the value modulo a positive modulus first (`x.mod(m).modInverse(m)`).

### Proof of concept

A negative public exponent passed to RSA key generation never returns (also with the callback form and with `createKeyPairGenerationState()` / `stepKeyPairGenerationState()`):

    var forge = require('node-forge');
    forge.pki.rsa.generateKeyPair({bits: 256, e: -1});  // hangs at 100% CPU

Calling `modInverse()` directly with a negative value or modulus hangs the same way:

    var BigInteger = forge.jsbn.BigInteger;
    new BigInteger('-1').modInverse(new BigInteger('7'));  // hangs
    new BigInteger('3').modInverse(new BigInteger('-7'));  // hangs

With the fix, these calls return zero. The regression tests are in `tests/unit/jsbn.js`.

### Impact

Applications are affected only if they:
- pass an untrusted value as the RSA public exponent `e` to `forge.pki.rsa.generateKeyPair()`, `forge.pki.rsa.createKeyPairGenerationState()` or `forge.pki.rsa.stepKeyPairGenerationState()`, or
- call `forge.jsbn.BigInteger#modInverse()` directly with negative values derived from untrusted input.

An attacker who can supply such a value makes the call hang indefinitely at 100% CPU, which blocks the Node.js event loop (denial of service). Keys and other data parsed by node-forge (DER, PEM, JWK, PKCS#12, X.509, TLS) cannot trigger this issue, and the documented usage of key generation passes a constant exponent (65537). ### Summary

forge.pkcs12.pkcs12FromAsn1() accepts a PKCS#12 MAC iteration count of zero (or less) from the input, and the PKCS#12 key derivation function then returns a constant key that does not depend on the password or salt. An attacker who does not know the password can modify a PKCS#12/PFX file and compute a MAC that verifies with any password; PKCS#12 PBE-encrypted private keys prepared the same way decrypt with any password. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`p12.pkcs12FromAsn1()` in `lib/pkcs12.js` reads the MAC iteration count (`MacData.iterations`) from the input and passes it to the PKCS#12 key derivation function `pki.pbe.generatePkcs12Key()` in `lib/pbe.js` (also exposed as `forge.pkcs12.generateKey()`) without checking that it is at least 1. The key derivation function (RFC 7292 Appendix B.2) runs its hash loop `iter` times. With an iteration count of 0 (or an empty or negative INTEGER), no hashing is done and the function returns the PKCS#12 diversifier ID byte repeated, for example `0x03` repeated 20 times for an HMAC-SHA1 MAC key. The result does not depend on the password or the salt, so anyone can compute a valid MAC over arbitrary PFX contents.

The same key derivation function is used by `pki.pbe.getCipherForPKCS12PBE()` for the PKCS#12 password-based encryption schemes `pbeWithSHAAnd3-KeyTripleDES-CBC` and `pbewithSHAAnd40BitRC2-CBC`, whose `pkcs-12PbeParams` iteration count is also read from the input. With an iteration count of 0 or less, the encryption key and IV are constants (`0x01` and `0x02` repeated). This is reached from shrouded key bags and encrypted SafeContents in `pkcs12FromAsn1()`, and from `forge.pki.decryptPrivateKeyInfo()` (for example for `ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY` PEM input).

RFC 7292 defines `MacData` with `iterations INTEGER DEFAULT 1`; an iteration count only makes sense as 1 or more (RFC 8018 uses `INTEGER (1..MAX)` for the same concept). PBES2 (PBKDF2) encrypted content is not affected.

The fix rejects iteration counts less than 1 when verifying a PKCS#12 MAC in `pkcs12FromAsn1()` ("PKCS#12 MAC iteration count must be >= 1.") and at the entry of `pki.pbe.generatePkcs12Key()` ("PKCS#12 key derivation iteration count must be >= 1."), which covers the MAC, both PKCS#12 PBE schemes and direct `forge.pkcs12.generateKey()` callers.

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Iteration counts less than 1 are now rejected when verifying a PKCS#12 MAC and in the PKCS#12 key derivation function.

### Workarounds
Before calling `forge.pkcs12.pkcs12FromAsn1()`, reject inputs whose `MacData.iterations` is present and less than 1. For encrypted private keys using the PKCS#12 PBE schemes, there is no simple workaround other than checking the `pkcs-12PbeParams` iteration count before decryption, or upgrading.

### Credits
Reported by Thai, Calif.io in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research.

### Proof of concept

Take any PKCS#12/PFX file, replace its AuthenticatedSafe with attacker-chosen content (for example the attacker's certificate and an unencrypted private key), set `MacData.iterations` to 0 (DER `02 01 00`), and compute the HMAC-SHA1 over the new content with the key `0x03` repeated 20 times. On node-forge <= 1.4.0, `forge.pkcs12.pkcs12FromAsn1(asn1, password)` reports successful MAC verification for whatever password the application supplies and returns the attacker's certificate and key. An empty or negative iteration count behaves the same way. Likewise, a shrouded key bag or `ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY` using `pbeWithSHAAnd3-KeyTripleDES-CBC` with iteration count 0 decrypts with any password.

The constant key is visible directly:

```js
var salt = new forge.util.ByteBuffer('anysalt');
forge.pkcs12.generateKey('any password', salt, 3, 0, 20).toHex();
// <= 1.4.0: '0303030303030303030303030303030303030303'
// 1.4.1: throws "PKCS#12 key derivation iteration count must be >= 1."
```

The fix adds regression tests in `tests/unit/pkcs12.js` and the reporter's PoC in `tests/pocs/`.

A connection created with `forge.tls.createConnection()` throws an uncaught `TypeError` from `process()` when it receives a record of another content type while waiting for the rest of a handshake message that was split across records. In `lib/tls.js`, `_readRecord()` handles a record that arrives while a handshake message split across records is incomplete. That fatal error closes and resets the connection, which sets `c.record` to `null`. `_readRecord()` then continues with `c.record.ready = true` and throws `TypeError: Cannot set properties of null (setting 'ready')` out of `process()`. The code is unchanged since the first release.

RFC 5246 section 6.2.1 allows a handshake message to be fragmented across records, and RFC 8446 section 5.1 forbids interleaving handshake messages with other record types. Failing the connection with `unexpected_message` is the intended behavior; the bug is the crash after the error.

The fix returns from `_readRecord()` right after the fatal error. The connection is failed, the alert is sent and the `error` callback is called as before, and `process()` no longer throws.

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. The connection still fails with a fatal `unexpected_message` alert and the `error` callback, but `process()` no longer throws.

### Workarounds
Wrap every call to `connection.process()` in `try`/`catch`. The connection has already been failed and closed when the exception is thrown, so the exception can be ignored or the socket destroyed.

### Summary

Connections created with `forge.tls.createConnection()` processed received TLS records recursively, one stack level per record. A peer can send one chunk of thousands of small records, such as heartbeat records, which are accepted before the handshake, and `process()` throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`, which terminates Node.js processes that use the documented socket wiring. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

In `lib/tls.js`, `c.process()` reads one record and passes it to `_update()`, which calls the handler for the record type from `ctTable`. Every handler (`tls.handleHeartbeat`, `tls.handleApplicationData`, `tls.handleHandshake` for fragmented messages, `tls.handleHelloRequest` and the other handshake handlers) ends by calling `c.process()` again to continue with the next buffered record, or the next message in the same record. Each record therefore adds `process` → `_update` → handler to the call stack. In Node.js 24, about 2,300 eight-byte records (under 20 KB) in one chunk are enough for `process()` to throw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`.

`ctTable` maps heartbeat records to `tls.handleHeartbeat` in every client and server state, so heartbeat records are processed before the handshake without any extension negotiation. The attack needs no authentication and no valid handshake messages. Both server connections (attacked by a client) and client connections (attacked by the server they connect to) are affected. Other record types recurse the same way: a handshake message fragmented over many records, many HelloRequest messages in one record, or many application data records after the handshake.

node-forge reports TLS protocol errors through the `error` callback, so applications do not normally wrap `process()` in `try`/`catch`. When `process()` is called from a Node.js socket `data` handler, as in the documented usage, the exception is uncaught and terminates the process. If the exception is caught, the connection is left partially processed and should be discarded.

No specification is violated; this is an implementation flaw (uncontrolled recursion).

The fix makes `c.process()` iterative. The record-reading code moves into `_processRecord()`, and `c.process()` runs it in a loop. A handler's call to `c.process()` without new data, made while records are being processed, now only flags that the loop should continue. Calls with new data are processed right away as before, so callback order and return values are unchanged.

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Records are now processed in a loop, so the stack depth no longer depends on the number of records.

### Workarounds
Wrap every call to `connection.process()` in `try`/`catch`, and on an exception close the connection (`connection.close()`) and destroy the underlying socket. This prevents the process crash but not the loss of the attacked connection.

### Credits
Reported jointly by Ziyue Wang, Chenchen, Strick Sheng, Liyi Zhou, and Maurice Ng.

  var rec = forge.util.hexToBytes('1803010003010000');
  c.process(new Array(5001).join(rec)); // 5,000 records, 40,000 bytes

### Summary
node-forge parses certificate extensions with the deprecated OIDs `2.5.29.10` and `2.5.29.13` as `basicConstraints`, and `forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain()` used the first extension with that name. A certificate with a forged deprecated-OID extension (`cA` TRUE) before its genuine `basicConstraints` extension (`cA` FALSE) is accepted as a CA certificate, and the same technique can hide a `pathLenConstraint`. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`lib/oids.js` maps the deprecated certificate extension OIDs `2.5.29.10` and `2.5.29.13` to the name `basicConstraints`, the same name as the RFC 5280 extension `2.5.29.19`. `certificateExtensionFromAsn1()` in `lib/x509.js` decodes extensions by name, so these extensions are decoded into the same `cA` and `pathLenConstraint` fields. `cert.getExtension()` returns the first extension with a matching name, and `pki.verifyCertificateChain()` looked up `basicConstraints` by name.

As a result, a certificate that contains a `2.5.29.10` (or `2.5.29.13`) extension with `cA` TRUE before its genuine `basicConstraints` extension with `cA` FALSE is accepted as a CA certificate. The same technique can hide a CA certificate's `pathLenConstraint`. A deprecated-OID extension on its own also satisfies the check added for GHSA-2328-f5f3-gj25 (CVE-2026-33896) that `basicConstraints` is present. RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.9 defines basicConstraints only as `id-ce 19` (`2.5.29.19`), and the path validation checks in section 6.1.4 apply to that extension.

The fix makes chain verification look up basicConstraints by OID (`cert.getExtension({id: '2.5.29.19'})`). This covers both the `cA` and the `pathLenConstraint` checks. Certificate parsing, the OID table and `cert.getExtension('basicConstraints')` are unchanged.

Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Chain verification now uses only the `basicConstraints` extension with OID `2.5.29.19`.

#### Workarounds
None in node-forge itself. Applications that pass an `options.verify` callback to `pki.verifyCertificateChain()` (or `verify` to `forge.tls.createConnection()`) can reject chains in which a non-leaf certificate has no `2.5.29.19` extension with `cA` TRUE, for example with `cert.getExtension({id: '2.5.29.19'})`. CA operators can avoid copying unrecognized extensions from certificate requests.

WorkOS Security Team· [security@workos.com](mailto:security@workos.com) (@nickcollisson-workos)

### Summary

When PHPT tests are run with code coverage, PHPUnit 13.4.0 to 13.4.3 writes the code of each PHPT test to a directory with a fixed name below the operating system's path used for temporary files, for instance `/tmp/phpunit-phpt` on Linux, and executes it from there. PHPUnit uses this directory even when it was created by another user.

On a system where the path used for temporary files is shared between users, another local user can create this directory before the developer runs PHPUnit, replace the code of a PHPT test before it is executed, and thereby execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the developer. The test still passes and the code coverage report is complete, so the attack is not visible.

The impact is full code execution as the user who runs PHPUnit. The likelihood is low: the attacker needs an account on the same system and must create the directory before the developer runs PHPT tests with code coverage. macOS and Windows use per-user temporary directories by default and are not affected in their default configuration. PHPUnit 12.5 and earlier are not affected.

### Details

When code coverage is collected for a PHPT test, PHPUnit writes two temporary files: a `.php` file with the code of the PHPT test (the "job" file), which the child process executes, and a `.coverage` file, to which the child process writes the code coverage data it collected.

Since PHPUnit 13.4.0, these files are created in a directory with a fixed name:

* [`TestCase::coverageFilesDirectory()`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/TestCase.php#L132-L143) returns `sys_get_temp_dir() . '/phpunit-phpt'`
* The [constructor](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/TestCase.php#L169-L174) names the files `phpunit_phpt_<random>.php` and `phpunit_phpt_<random>.coverage` in this directory

Before a PHPT test is run with code coverage, this directory is [created using `Filesystem::createDirectory()`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/TestCase.php#L319). [`Filesystem::createDirectory()`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Util/Filesystem.php#L27-L30) returns `true` when the directory already exists, without checking its owner or its permissions. When it does not exist, it is created with mode `0777` (subject to the umask).

[`Renderer::renderForCoverage()`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/Renderer.php#L112) then writes the job file using `file_put_contents()`. The child process loads Composer's autoloader, the bootstrap script, and the code coverage driver, and then [executes the job file using `require`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/templates/phpt.tpl#L43).

When another user created the directory, that user owns it. The owner of a directory can list its contents and rename, delete, or replace every file in it, regardless of who owns the file. The directory does not have the sticky bit set, so protections such as Linux's `fs.protected_regular` and `fs.protected_symlinks` do not apply either. The random part of the file names therefore does not prevent the attack: the attacker waits for the job file to appear, renames it, and puts a file with their own code in its place. The attacker's code can then execute the original job file, so that the test passes and the code coverage report is complete.

The `.coverage` file can be replaced in the same way. [`TestCase::cleanupForCoverage()`](https://github.com/sebastianbergmann/phpunit/blob/13.4.3/src/Runner/Phpt/TestCase.php#L760-L803) only allows objects of PHPUnit's class for raw code coverage data to be unserialized from it, so this only allows the falsification of code coverage data.
